Making the rocks follow the sky mode

The sky and the clouds already change with sunrise, day, sunset and night. The rocks don't: they keep their bright daylight look in every mode. Here's every rock involved, the possible fixes, and a live preview using your real rock images. Nothing in the site has been changed.

There's already a pattern to copy: the clouds change per mode from one list in lib/theme/palette.ts, and every mode change animates over the same 0.9 s crossfade. The 3D clouds swap their light colours; the flat cloud images get a per-mode CSS filter. The rocks just need an entry in that same list.

The options

A · CSS filter per mode

Each rock image gets a filter per mode (darker, desaturated and pushed blue at night; warmer at sunrise and sunset). This is exactly what the flat cloud images already do.

  • Good: smallest change; reuses an existing pattern; no extra files; animates with the crossfade.
  • Weak: a filter treats every pixel the same, so night looks like a dimmed daytime photo, not a rock lit by the night sky. Tuning a blue cast with sepia + hue-rotate is fiddly and can turn muddy.

B · Sky-tinted light (recommended)

A thin colour layer sits on each rock, cut to the rock's own shape, and multiplies its colour into the rock: a top-to-bottom gradient taken from the mode's sky. At night it's moonlit navy, darker at the base; at sunset, lavender to amber. In day mode it's white, which changes nothing.

  • Good: the rock reads as lit by the sky above it, not just darkened, because the tint varies with height like the sky does. The colours are two CSS variables the existing theme code already animates, so it crossfades in step with the sky and clouds with no new animation loop. No extra image downloads (the tint reuses the rock image as its cut-out shape).
  • Cost: one extra layer per rock and a blend mode. It's static once the crossfade ends, so there's no ongoing cost.
  • Limit: it can colour and shade the rock, but it can't add new light, like a moonlit rim. That's option C's job.

C · Baked art per mode

A separately graded version of each rock image for each mode. On a mode change, the page crossfades between them. The preview's night version was graded offline from your current images: moonlit colour, a darker base, and a soft moonlight rim on the side facing the sky.

  • Good: best possible look; any lighting you like (rims, glints, shadows); no runtime cost beyond a fade.
  • Cost: 4 modes × 5 rock images = up to 20 files to make and maintain (~60–180 KB each). Every future rock change multiplies. Files for modes not in use should load only on a switch, so the first switch needs preloading to avoid a flash.
  • Middle ground: bake night only (the mode where B falls shortest) and use B for sunrise and sunset.

D · Real-time relighting (not recommended)

Draw the cliffs in WebGL with normal maps and real lights. That's the most flexible, but it means generating normal maps for painted art, a new full-height WebGL layer, and the heavy-effect rules (GPU budget, quality tiers), for something B and C already cover.

Recommendation

  1. B for every flat rock image: hero cliffs, grass hover, footer rocks. Add a rock entry (two tint colours) to each mode in palette.ts; the theme code animates them alongside the sky colours.
  2. The two WebGL places follow the same palette: the intro rock planes multiply by the same two tint colours in their shader, so they still match the page rocks pixel for pixel when the intro hands off. The testimonial rocks get per-mode light colours and a sky reflection map rebuilt from the mode's sky, the way the 3D clouds already do it.
  3. Optional polish: if night still feels flat after B, bake a night version (C) of the hero and footer rocks only.

Compare the options in the preview at Night and Sunset; those modes show the differences most. Tick "Show the grass version" to check that the hover grass would follow too.
